segments.english: After these events the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision, saying: Do not be afraid, Abram. I am a shield for you; your reward is very great.
segments.literal: after the-things the-these came word-of LORD to Abram in-the-vision to-say not you-fear Abram I shield to-you your-reward making-great exceedingly

tokens.note: Rashi (after Bereshit Rabbah): אחר marks closeness in time, אחרי a remote interval
דְּבָרִים is 'matters, events' here, not 'words'
'the word of the LORD came to' is the formula for a prophetic communication
construct state before the divine name
מַחֲזֶה, from חזה 'see': a prophetic vision (Ibn Ezra: במראות הנבואה)
לֵאמֹר, infinitive construct with ל: introduces direct speech
אַל with the jussive form is the usual prohibition
no verb: a verbless clause, so present time by default
the pack parses the suffix as feminine; the form לָךְ is pausal, the suffix is the masculine ךְ with a pausal vowel on a masculine addressee (Abram)
construct form שְׂכָר- with suffix
infinitive absolute of the hifil functioning as a predicate: 'is made abundant'

phrases.literal: 'after the-things the-these'; Rashi reads אחר as 'directly after'

phrases.english: the word of the LORD came to Abram
phrases.literal: 'came word-of LORD to Abram'; English moves the subject before the verb
'in-the-vision'; the article is rendered by the indefinite in English

phrases.english: I am a shield for you

phrases.literal: 'your-reward making-great exceedingly'; infinitive absolute as predicate

grammar: הָיָה דְבַר־יְהֹוָה אֶל־: the standard formula for the arrival of a prophetic word. Here it is joined to בַּמַּחֲזֶה, a rare word for the medium of the revelation.

The two sentences אָנֹכִי מָגֵן לָךְ and שְׂכָרְךָ הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד are verbless. The English present tense is a choice: Ibn Ezra takes the first as a past 'I was a shield' (see commentary), but the Hebrew has no tense.
הַרְבֵּה is the hifil infinitive absolute of רבה used as a predicate adjective ('abundant'); it can also be read adverbially or as a noun clause, 'your reward: to make very many'.
The zaqef qaton on לָךְ and the pashta on אָנֹכִי divide the speech: prohibition, then the two grounds for it.
segments.note: The speech is placed in a vision (בַּמַּחֲזֶה), which Ibn Ezra glosses as 'the visions of prophecy' and Radak says shows Abram an action, not only words. The present tense of 'I am a shield' leaves open Ibn Ezra's past reading; the Hebrew has no verb.

commentary.summary: Rashi: אחר means close in time (אחרי a remote interval). The reference is to the victory over the kings: Abram feared he had used up his reward or would be punished for the lives he took, so God says 'I am a shield' against punishment and 'your reward is great'.
Ibn Ezra: בַּמַּחֲזֶה means in the sights (visions) of prophecy, so the English 'in a vision'.

Ibn Ezra reads אָנֹכִי מָגֵן לָךְ as past, 'I was a shield to you and saved you from the kings, and I will also give you a reward because you went out to rescue your nephew with a few men and relied on me'. The English keeps the Hebrew's tenseless clause.
Ramban: Abram feared two things, that the kings would return with larger forces, or that he would die without offspring; God's promise of a shield answers the first and the reward the second.
Radak: שכרך הרבה מאד, 'great in this world and very great in the world to come'. The English does not split הרבה and מאד between two worlds.

apparatus: The pack parses לָךְ as having a feminine suffix; the pausal ָךְ is the pausal form of the masculine suffix, since Abram is addressed. The data is kept.
Onkelos has 'my Memra will be a strong shield for you' (מֵימְרִי תְּקוֹף לָךְ), a paraphrase of the shield image; it does not change the Hebrew sense.

segments.english: Abram said, My Lord, the LORD, what will you give me, when I go on childless, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus?
segments.literal: and-said Abram my-lord LORD what you-will-give to-me and-I going childless and-son-of Meshek my-house he Damascus Eliezer

tokens.note: wayyiqtol, narrative past
אֲדֹנָי: plural of majesty with first-person suffix, used only of God
written יהוה with the vowels of אֱלֹהִים (יֱהֹוִה) so that אֲדֹנָי is read before it
circumstantial waw: 'when I ...'
participle of הלך: 'am walking'; Ramban records the sense 'am passing away', and the pack lists Qal II.1 for that
עֲרִירִי: Rashi, citing Menahem, 'without an heir'; Ibn Ezra, like the Targum, 'without a child'
construct state, בֶּן־מֶשֶׁק: 'son of Meshek'
hapax: root שׁקק per Ibn Ezra and Radak; Rashi and the Targum 'one who manages, steward'
resumptive pronoun: 'he is ...'
דַּמֶּשֶׂק with the sequence; Rashi: the Targum takes it 'from Damascus'; Radak: a yod of relation (דַּמַּשְׂקִי) is missing
name meaning 'God is help'

phrases.literal: 'my-lords LORD'; the decisions file gives 'the LORD' for the name

phrases.english: and the steward of my house
phrases.literal: 'and-son-of Meshek my-house'; Rashi after the Targum: one on whose word the whole house is fed, my steward

grammar: וְאָנֹכִי הוֹלֵךְ עֲרִירִי: a circumstantial clause with a participle ('while I am going about without ...'). The sense of הוֹלֵךְ ('go on living' or 'go to my death') is open, see the note.

בֶּן־מֶשֶׁק בֵּיתִי הוּא דַּמֶּשֶׂק אֱלִיעֶזֶר: a difficult verse. מֶשֶׁק is a hapax, understood by Rashi and the Targum as 'one who manages (my house)', by Ibn Ezra as from שׁקק 'run about'. The English follows the sense 'steward' which both give.
אֲדֹנָי יֱהֹוִה: the Masoretic pointing יֱהֹוִה tells the reader to say Elohim, not Adonai, after אֲדֹנָי. Radak says the title precedes the name because the name is the essence.
The etnaḥta on עֲרִירִי divides the verse between Abram's complaint and its explanation.
segments.note: דַּמֶּשֶׂק אֱלִיעֶזֶר is rendered 'Eliezer of Damascus' with the Targum and Radak (who supplies the missing relational yod). Another reading in Radak is that the man's own name was Damascus. For הוֹלֵךְ the English keeps the neutral 'go on'.

commentary.summary: Rashi gives Menahem's view that עֲרִירִי means 'without an heir' (as ובכל תבואתי תשרש) and his own view that it comes from the root of 'destruction'; both come out as 'without children', which the English uses.
Rashi, after the Targum: בן משק ביתי is the one by whose word the whole house is fed (על פיך ישק), my steward; had Abram a son, he would be in charge of Abram's property. The English 'steward'.

Rashi: by the Targum he was from Damascus; by the midrash Abram pursued the kings as far as Damascus. The Talmud reads דמשק as an acrostic, 'he draws and gives drink from his master's teaching to others'. The English takes the plain sense, 'of Damascus'.
Ibn Ezra: the yod of עֲרִירִי is like that in אכזרי and is dropped in ערירים יהיו; the sense is as the Targum says, 'without a child'.

Ibn Ezra: מֶשֶׁק has the pattern of מכס, from the doubled root of שוקק, 'a son who draws himself and another with him'. The English 'steward' is the sense of the Targum he also cites, but his derivation is kept here.
Radak: the yod of relation is missing, so דַּמֶּשֶׂק means 'the Damascene' like שבט הימני; or his name was Damascus and Abram named him Eliezer. The English takes the first.
Ramban notes Rashi's older commentators read הולך ערירי as 'I am going to my death childless' (like הולך האדם אל בית עולמו) and prefers 'wandering childless'. The English 'go on' keeps both.

apparatus: Onkelos: 'and the steward (בַּר פַּרְנָסָא) of my house, he is Eliezer the Damascene'.
The pack gives the lemma אֲדֹנָי with parse 'plural, construct' and the name יהוה with the pointing יֱהֹוִה; both are kept.

segments.english: Abram said, Look, you have given me no offspring, and so a member of my household is my heir.
segments.literal: and-said Abram lo to-me not you-gave seed and-behold son-of my-house inheriting me

tokens.note: הֵן, a variant of הִנֵּה: 'see!', introduces a complaint
perfect, 2nd person masculine singular, with the final -ta written with a mappiq-like ending נָתַתָּה
זֶרַע is a collective: 'seed'
וְהִנֵּה: 'and look', draws attention to the consequence
בֶּן־בֵּיתִי, 'son of my house', one born or brought up in the house
participle, 'is inheriting', either a present state or imminent future
אֹתִי: the object marker with suffix, 'inheriting me', i.e. taking my place

phrases.english: you have given me no offspring
phrases.literal: 'to-me not you-gave seed'; the fronted 'to me' marks the contrast with what was promised
'inheriting me'; the participle with the object marker, 'will take my place'

grammar: הֵן לִי לֹא נָתַתָּה זָרַע: 'to me you have not given seed'. The word order puts 'to me' first, against the promises Abram has heard.

וְהִנֵּה בֶן־בֵּיתִי יוֹרֵשׁ אֹתִי: the participle יוֹרֵשׁ describes a state near at hand. Verbs of inheriting normally take the thing inherited as object, not the person, so 'inheriting me' means 'inheriting from me'.
זֶרַע is singular but collective, 'offspring', and the English uses a singular noun for it.
segments.note: Rashi takes the opening as asking 'what good is all that you give me?', continuing the complaint of verse 2. The English keeps the sentence as a complaint with 'Look'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'and what use is all that you might give me?' - the sentence is a complaint carrying on from מה תתן לי.
Radak: בֶּן בֵּיתִי is one Abram esteems as his own seed, as Eliezer who ruled all he had; hence 'you have given me no seed'.
Sforno: even if You give me a child later, he would be too young to manage the property, and the steward of the house would be the heir in practice.

apparatus: Onkelos: 'behold, to me you have given no child, and behold the son of my house is inheriting me (יָרִית יָתִי)'.

segments.english: Then the word of the LORD came to him, saying: This man will not be your heir; but rather one who comes from your own body will be your heir.
segments.literal: and-behold word-of LORD to-him to-say not he-will-inherit-you this but-if who he-will-come-out from-your-innards he he-will-inherit-you

tokens.note: וְהִנֵּה: 'and behold', the narrator marks the sudden arrival of the word (Ramban: while Abram was still speaking)
imperfect with 2nd person suffix: 'will inherit you'; the first one marks the accent on the verb
זֶה, demonstrative, 'this one', i.e. Eliezer
כִּי־אִם together: 'but only', 'but rather', after a negative
מֵעֶה, plural 'innards': a euphemism for the organ of begetting (Ibn Ezra, Radak)
resumes the relative clause

phrases.literal: 'to-him'; the verb is not written and is supplied from the context

phrases.english: This man will not be your heir

phrases.literal: 'but-if'; the idiom כִּי אִם after a negative

phrases.english: one who comes from your own body
phrases.literal: 'who he-will-come-out from-your-innards'; Ibn Ezra: a euphemism for the organ nearest

grammar: וְהִנֵּה דְבַר־יְהֹוָה אֵלָיו: a verbless clause, 'and behold, the word of the LORD to him'; the qadma on וְהִנֵּה marks it as the start of a new sentence in answer to Abram's last words.
לֹא יִירָשְׁךָ זֶה: the verb has the 2nd person masculine suffix and the same verb occurs again at the end, so the verse is built around a contrast between two heirs.
כִּי־אִם after a negative means 'but rather', not 'if'.
יִירָשׁ with an object of person means 'be the heir of' that person, here 'inherit from you'.
segments.note: מֵעֶיךָ is rendered 'your own body', keeping the euphemism that Ibn Ezra identifies (Radak adds that it is the 'vessel of seed', cf. צאצאי מעיך Isaiah 48:19).

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: מִמֵּעֶיךָ is a 'kinuy', a euphemism for the limb, because it is near; hence 'from your own body'.
Ramban: וְהִנֵּה means that while Abram was still speaking the word of the LORD came suddenly; the promise here concerns only the inheritance, not the reward.
Radak: the verse limits the earlier promise, 'to you and to your seed', to a true descendant who comes from your innards.

apparatus: Onkelos: 'This one will not inherit you, but one whom you will beget, he will inherit you.'

segments.english: He brought him outside and said, Look toward the sky, please, and count the stars, if you are able to count them. Then he said to him, So will your offspring be.
segments.literal: and-brought-out him the-outside and-said look please the-heavenward and-count the-stars if you-are-able to-count them and-said to-him thus he-will-be your-seed

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of the hifil of יצא: 'caused to go out'
הַחוּצָה: with the directional ה, 'to the outside'
doubled pashta on the verb
imperative of the hifil of נבט; Rashi hears in it 'look down from above'
נָא is a particle of entreaty or politeness
directional ה on שָׁמַיִם: 'skyward'
אִם opens a conditional clause; it also introduces an indirect question, 'whether you can'
a second wayyiqtol of אמר, marking a new utterance after the etnaḥta
כֹּה: 'thus', pointing to the stars

phrases.literal: 'and-brought-out him the-outside'; Rashi and Ramban: from his tent, to see the stars

phrases.english: if you are able to count them
phrases.literal: 'if you-are-able to-count them'; the אֵת marks the object of the verb

grammar: וַיּוֹצֵא אֹתוֹ הַחוּצָה: a hifil wayyiqtol. The subject is God, the object Abram. הַחוּצָה has the article and the directional ה together.
הַבֶּט־נָא הַשָּׁמַיְמָה: the directional ה on שָׁמַיִם is a rare spelling of the same ending. The imperative with נָא is courteous.
אִם־תּוּכַל לִסְפֹּר: אִם introduces a conditional clause whose result is implied (the answer is no). The verb סָפַר is used twice (imperative and infinitive) in the one speech.
כֹּה יִהְיֶה זַרְעֶךָ: the adverb כֹּה refers to the stars in sight; the verb is future and 'offspring' is collective.
The two disjunctive pashta marks on וַיֹּאמֶר show that the speech is a single unit; the etnaḥta on אֹתָם ends the first speech, and the second begins with a new וַיֹּאמֶר.
segments.note: Rashi gives the plain sense (God took Abram out of his tent to see the stars) and the midrash (go out of your astrology; 'look down' from above the stars). The English follows the plain sense, with the midrashic alternatives recorded.

commentary.summary: Rashi: by its plain sense He brought him out of his tent to see the stars. By the midrash He told him, go out of your astrology, since you saw in the constellations that you will not have a son: 'Abram has no son, but Abraham will; Sarai will not bear, but Sarah will'. Another midrash lifted him above the stars, hence the sense of looking down.

Radak: the word came to him in his tent, and in the vision He brought him outside, as in Ezekiel 8:3 'he brought me to Jerusalem in visions of God'. The stars after the dust of the earth in the earlier promise are both hyperbole.
Ramban repeats Rashi's plain sense and the midrash, and notes that Abram had by now fathered Ishmael, so the midrash is explained as meaning that Abram sought an heir by Sarai.

apparatus: Onkelos: 'and he brought him out and said, Look now at the heavens and count the stars, if you are able to count them; and he said to him, So will your children be.'

segments.english: He trusted in the LORD, and the LORD reckoned it to him as righteousness.

tokens.note: a perfect with וְ in a narrative sequence; an unusual form of continuing narrative that marks a state, 'and he was trusting'; the hifil of אמן takes בְּ for the object of trust
the Variants list notes that WLC points the divine name differently; the base text is kept
wayyiqtol with a feminine suffix: the 'it' is his trust (a feminine noun implied); the subject is God, by Rashi

phrases.english: and the LORD reckoned it to him
phrases.literal: 'and-he-reckoned-it to-him'; the English names the subject, which Rashi takes to be the LORD; Ramban's second reading takes Abram as the subject and the promise as the 'it'
'righteousness'; Ibn Ezra: 'a merit', as in וּצְדָקָה תִּהְיֶה לָּנוּ, Deuteronomy 6:25

grammar: וְהֶאֱמִן: the waw with a perfect (weqatal) after a string of wayyiqtols; it gives the narrator's comment on Abram's state of trust, not a new event in the sequence. The hifil of אמן means 'consider firm', 'put trust in'.
וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לּוֹ צְדָקָה: the verb takes an object suffix (feminine, 'it') and a double complement, 'to him' and 'as righteousness'. The feminine suffix refers to his faith or to the promise.
The subject of וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ is not named. Rashi and Sforno take it to be God; Ramban records a second reading in which Abram counts the promise as God's righteousness (cf. Psalm 106:31 of Pinhas).
segments.note: The English names the LORD as the subject of 'reckoned', following Rashi and Sforno; the ambiguity of the Hebrew (Abram, or God) is kept in the phrase note and the commentary. צְדָקָה is 'righteousness' (Ibn Ezra: a merit, as in Deuteronomy 6:25).

commentary.summary: Rashi: Abram did not ask for a sign about this (the son); but about inheriting the land he asked for a sign, 'by what shall I know'. So 'he trusted' refers to the son.

Rashi: the Holy One, blessed be He, counted it to Abram as merit and as righteousness for the trust he showed. A second reading takes בַּמָּה אֵדַע as asking in what merit Israel will endure, and God answers, by the merit of sacrifices.
Ibn Ezra: צדקה is as in וצדקה תהיה לנו (Deuteronomy 6:25) and like צדק ומשפט; he adds that the Sages' sense of צדקה as charity is different.

Ramban does not understand Rashi's 'merit' (why would Abram not trust a God of truth?), and suggests Abram trusted that God would give him a child out of His own righteousness, not Abram's; or that God counted the promise itself as righteousness.
Radak: God counted the complete trust as righteousness and uprightness of heart, since he and his wife were growing old and the promise was delayed, and yet he trusted.

apparatus: The pack's Variants note: WLC reads בַּֽיהוָ֑ה where the base (MAM) writes בַּֽיהֹוָ֑ה; the same name, no difference in sense.
Onkelos: 'and he trusted in the Memra of the LORD, and He counted it to him as merit (לְזָכוּ)'.

segments.english: He said to him, I am the LORD who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to take possession of it.
segments.literal: and-said to-him I LORD who I-brought-you-out from-Ur Chaldeans to-give to-you [object-mark] the-land the-this to-possess-it

tokens.note: hifil perfect, 1st person, with 2nd person masculine suffix
כַּשְׂדִּים is a gentilic: 'of the Kasdim'; the familiar English form is 'Chaldeans'
infinitive construct of נתן: the final nun drops and the ת is doubled in לָתֵת form
אֶת marks the definite object of the infinitive
infinitive construct with a feminine suffix: 'to possess it'; the ת is the feminine ending of the infinitive of ירשׁ

phrases.english: who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans

phrases.literal: the object marker has no English counterpart
'to-possess-it'; Radak and Sforno: that his sons may inherit it from him as an unbroken inheritance

grammar: אֲנִי יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ: the formula of self-introduction, 'I am the LORD who ...', that recalls the earlier act as grounds for the promise.
The relative אֲשֶׁר takes a 1st person verb, 'who I brought you out', and the English turns it into a normal relative clause with 'who brought'.
לָתֶת לְךָ ... לְרִשְׁתָּהּ: two infinitives with ל expressing purpose. The first is of נתן, the second of ירשׁ with the feminine suffix referring to הָאָרֶץ.
The tevir on לְךָ and the darga on לָתֶת set 'to give you' against 'this land ... to possess it'.
segments.note: אוּר כַּשְׂדִּים is rendered 'Ur of the Chaldeans', the familiar English name; Ibn Ezra points out that the promise names Ur and not Haran because it was in Ur that the call came, as the Lekh Lekha section shows.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: it says Ur and not Haran as proof that the call is told in the Lekh Lekha section and was given there, as he explained at that place; so the English keeps 'Ur of the Chaldeans'.

Ibn Ezra: Abram trusted God that his son would inherit; for the inheritance of the land he asked for a sign, as Gideon did, since every prophecy is conditional unless sworn. It bears on verse 8 and the sense of 'by what will I know', not on this verse.
Ramban: 'from the time I brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans and did a miracle for you, it was My will to give you this land'; not yet a decree, so Abram feared that the land depended on works.
Radak: I did not bring you out for nothing but to give you this land to inherit, meaning that his sons will inherit it, like an inheritance a man leaves to his sons.
Sforno on לְרִשְׁתָּהּ: so that the sons will inherit it from you by an inheritance that has no end.

apparatus: Onkelos: 'I am the LORD who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to inherit it.'

segments.english: He said, My Lord, the LORD, by what will I know that I shall take possession of it?
segments.literal: and-said my-lord LORD by-what I-will-know that I-will-possess-it

tokens.note: wayyiqtol; the subject is Abram, as the vocative that follows shows
plural of majesty with 1st person suffix
pointed יֱהֹוִה so that the reader says Elohim after אֲדֹנָי
בַּמָּה: ב with the interrogative מָה, 'by what means?'
imperfect, 1st person; cohortative sense, 'am I to know'

tokens.gloss: I shall take possession of it
tokens.note: imperfect with a feminine suffix referring to the land; Radak: 'my sons will inherit it', cf. Genesis 48:22

phrases.english: that I shall take possession of it

grammar: בַּמָּה אֵדַע: the interrogative with ב asks for the means or sign by which knowledge will come; it is not a statement of doubt, and Radak says Abram did not doubt that his sons would inherit.
כִּי אִירָשֶׁנָּה: the כִּי introduces the content of the knowledge, 'that I shall inherit it'. The suffix -נָּה, with the nun, is an energic form on a feminine object.
The etnaḥta on וַיֹּאמַר, with the lengthened form וַיֹּאמַר, sets the speech apart from the narrative.
segments.note: There are no normative comments on this verse. Radak and Sforno agree that Abram asks for knowledge that the inheritance will be lasting, since his descendants might sin and lose the land; the English 'by what will I know' keeps the question open, as the Hebrew does.

commentary.summary: Radak: Abram did not doubt that his sons would inherit, for he had trusted the LORD (15:6); he asked whether they would inherit it for ever, since they might sin and be exiled, and 'by what' asks in what way it will be made known to him, as the stars were shown for the offspring.
Sforno: perhaps the sons will sin and not be worthy to inherit.
Sforno says Abram did not retract his faith in this question; otherwise it would not have been counted to him as righteousness (Ezekiel 18:24).

apparatus: Onkelos: 'and he said, LORD God, by what shall I know that I will inherit it?' (בְּמָה אִדַּע אֲרֵי אֵרְתִינַהּ).
